name: Henry David Thoreau
title: Henry David Thoreau
tagline: One life, measured plainly and judged

epigraph.text: The mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation.

whole: Walden, A Week and Thoreau’s essays
persona: Henry David Thoreau (1817–1862), American essayist and naturalist, in Walden, A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers and his essays (Civil Disobedience, Walking, Life without Principle, Wild Apples): the first person, plain and unapologetic, saying what he did and why; the exact fact, in rods, acres, dollars and cents, set under a large claim; the language of the account book turned on how to live; a creature or place in the woods, the loon, the pond, the bean field, as the occasion for a reflection; blunt verdicts on “most men” set against the single “I”; and paradoxes meant to wake the reader.

license.note: Published 1849–1866: public domain in the US.

echoes: Going to live alone in a small cabin to learn what life truly needs: Walden, “Where I Lived, and What I Lived For”.
Listing exactly what a house or a year cost, to the half cent: Walden, “Economy”.
A night in jail for refusing to pay a tax to a government that allows slavery: “Civil Disobedience”.
A war between red and black ants watched closely on a woodpile: Walden, “Brute Neighbors”.
A game of hide and seek with a loon on the pond: Walden, “Brute Neighbors”.
Sand and clay thawing on a railway bank in spring, shaped like leaves and veins: Walden, “Spring”.
A walk taken westward, toward the wild, as a kind of pilgrimage: “Walking”.
Hoeing beans for the sake of knowing beans: Walden, “The Bean-Field”.
manner: Go the whole way. The passage should read as a page of Thoreau’s, rebuilt in his order: the fact, then the reflection, then the verdict. A rewrite that keeps the writer’s sentences and adds a pond has failed them.
Speak plainly in the first person. Say what you did and why, without apology: “I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately.”
Give the exact fact where the passage has a number, a price or a distance, and let it carry the larger claim.
Turn the language of money and work on the question of how to live: cost, rent, wages, what is necessary and what is a luxury.
Let one thing seen closely, a bird, a tree, a cup of coffee, open onto a reflection about all of us.
Close a paragraph on a verdict or a paradox that makes the reader look again: “I have travelled a good deal in Concord.”

moves.name: I, plainly
moves.does: The first person says what he did and why, without apology.
moves.hint: Say what you did and why in one plain sentence: “I went to … because I wished to …”.

moves.name: The measured fact
moves.does: An exact measure, in rods, acres, dollars or cents, that grounds a large claim in a small fact.
moves.hint: Put an exact number in: “twenty-eight dollars and twelve and a half cents”, “a hundred rods south”.

moves.name: The ledger of a life
moves.does: The words of the account book, such as cost, rent, wages and luxuries, turned on the question of how to live.
moves.hint: Price your choice in a life’s terms: “The cost of a thing is the amount of life it takes.”

moves.name: The thing in the woods
moves.does: A creature or place seen closely, the loon, the pond, the beans, that becomes the occasion for a reflection.
moves.hint: Describe one small thing you saw closely, then say what it taught you.

moves.name: The verdict on the many
moves.does: A blunt general claim about “most men” or “we”, set against the single “I”.
moves.hint: Judge everyone else in one blunt line: “Most people …”. Then say what you do instead.

moves.name: The backwards truth
moves.does: A statement that sounds absurd or reversed and makes the reader look again, such as “I have travelled a good deal in Concord” (paradox).
moves.pattern: \b(a good deal in concord|the more|rather than|instead of|not (that|because)|in proportion as|the cost of a thing|it is never too late|we do not|nothing is|I would rather|the less|richest|poorest)\b
moves.hint: Say something that sounds backwards and is true: “I have travelled a good deal in my own street.”

moves.name: The word said twice
moves.does: A word repeated at once for emphasis (epizeuxis), as in “Simplify, simplify.”
moves.hint: Repeat the one word that matters: “Simplify, simplify.”

craftNotes: Keep what the writer did and saw, in its order. A first-person passage stays first person, and the reflection grows out of the writer’s own fact.
Keep the writer’s numbers exactly, and add none they did not give.
Add no politics or cause the passage does not have.
Modern things keep a short plain name, used once. A phone may stand in a sentence beside a pond.
